Flesh (Biblical)
flesh
n.
“Flesh” from Old English flæsc; rendering the Hebrew bāsār and Greek sarx, which range from the physical body to human weakness to the sinful nature.

📖 Biblical Definition

“Flesh” (Hebrew bāsār, Greek sarx) is a richly varied biblical term whose meaning must be discerned from its context, ranging from the literal physical body to human nature in its weakness and creatureliness to—most significantly in Paul—the sinful nature or principle of corruption that wars against the Spirit. In its most basic sense, ‘flesh’ means the soft tissue of the body, or the body itself, or by extension all living creatures (‘all flesh’) and human kinship (‘my bone and my flesh’); in this sense flesh is not evil but simply creaturely—and the Word was made flesh, taking our true humanity, without any taint of sin. From this the term extends to denote human nature in its frailty, mortality, and limitation as contrasted with God and His Spirit: ‘all flesh is grass’; ‘the flesh profiteth nothing’; ‘flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom.’ But Paul gives the word a further, ethical sense that has become central to Christian theology: ‘the flesh’ as the sinful nature, the seat and principle of indwelling corruption that remains in the believer and wars against the Spirit. In this sense the flesh is not the body as such (sin is not located in matter, as the Gnostics thought) but the whole fallen self in its rebellion against God—‘the carnal mind is enmity against God’; ‘in my flesh dwelleth no good thing’; ‘the works of the flesh’ include not only bodily sins but envy, strife, idolatry, and heresy. The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; the believer is to walk in the Spirit and not fulfill the lust of the flesh, to mortify the deeds of the body, and to make no provision for the flesh. The careful interpreter must therefore distinguish these senses: to confuse the ethical ‘flesh’ (the sinful nature) with the physical body is to fall into the ancient error of despising the body and locating sin in matter, when Scripture locates it in the fallen heart and will. Rightly understood, ‘flesh’ teaches the goodness of the body God made and the incarnation took, the frailty of the creature before God, and—in its deepest sense—the corruption of the fallen nature against which the Christian wages lifelong war by the Spirit.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FLESH variously—the muscular part of the body, all animals, mankind, human nature, and the corrupt or carnal nature opposed to the Spirit.

expand to see more

FLESH, n. — ...4. The body of man, as distinguished from the soul. 5. Animal nature; the carnal appetites. 6. The corruptible body of man, or the present life. 7. The depraved nature of man; the carnal nature; the lusts. 8. Kindred; stock; family. 9. In Scripture, mankind; human nature.

FLESHLY, a. — Carnal; worldly; lascivious; pertaining to the flesh or its lusts.

📖 Key Scripture

John 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us..."

Galatians 5:17 — "For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other."

Romans 7:18 — "For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing."

Romans 8:8 — "So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The biblical “flesh” is corrupted by the Gnostic and ascetic error that equates it with the physical body—locating sin in matter and despising the body—rather than in the fallen nature, the rebellious self.

expand to see more

The most serious corruption of the biblical ‘flesh’ is the confusion of its ethical sense (the sinful nature) with the physical body, an error rooted in Greek and Gnostic dualism. If ‘the flesh’ that wars against the Spirit is identified with the material body, then sin is located in matter, the body becomes the enemy and the seat of corruption, and the spiritual life is reduced to the soul’s struggle to escape or subdue the flesh-as-body. From this error flowed the harsh asceticism that punished the body as evil, the contempt of marriage and bodily pleasures as inherently sinful, and ultimately the Gnostic and docetic denials that God could truly take flesh. But Scripture refutes this decisively: the Word was made flesh without sin, the body is the temple of the Spirit, and the ‘works of the flesh’ Paul lists include sins of the mind and spirit—idolatry, envy, strife, heresy—that have nothing to do with the body. Sin dwells not in matter but in the fallen heart and will.

The doctrine of the flesh, rightly understood, requires the careful discernment of its several senses according to context. Sometimes ‘flesh’ means simply the body or human kind, and is not evil but creaturely—the good creation God made and the Son assumed. Sometimes it denotes human frailty and mortality before the eternal God—‘all flesh is grass.’ And sometimes, especially in Paul, it denotes ‘the flesh’ in the ethical sense: the principle of indwelling sin, the whole fallen self in rebellion against God, the corruption that remains in the believer and wars against the Spirit. To read the body wherever Paul means the sinful nature is to misunderstand the Christian life as a war against matter rather than against sin, and to slander the good body God made. The believer’s warfare is not against his body but against the flesh in this deeper sense—the rebellious self—which he is to mortify by the Spirit, walking in the Spirit so that he does not fulfill the lusts of the flesh, until the corruption that now indwells him is finally abolished in glory.

Usage

"‘Flesh’ in Scripture ranges from the body, to human frailty, to the sinful nature—the sense must be read from context."

"Paul’s ‘flesh’ that wars against the Spirit is the fallen nature, not the body—sin dwells in the heart, not in matter."

"To equate the ethical ‘flesh’ with the physical body is the Gnostic error that despises the body God made and the Son assumed."
